article.title: Tulane Physicists Explain Why Gold Resists Tarnishing, Finding Surface Atoms Rearrange to Choke Off Oxidation
article.summary: A Physical Review Letters study finds gold's surface atoms reconstruct into denser patterns that slow oxidation by a billion to a trillion times.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

Gold jewelry can stay bright for centuries while other metals corrode within years, and a new study from Tulane University offers an explanation grounded in atomic-scale physics rather than gold's famous unreactivity alone. According to [ScienceDaily](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/07/260710003511.htm), researchers found that atoms on gold's surface reorganize themselves into protective configurations that suppress oxidation by a factor of a billion to a trillion.

## What We Know

The study, published in *Physical Review Letters* under the title "Role of Reconstruction in the Inertness of Gold toward Oxygen," was authored by Santu Biswas, a postdoctoral fellow, and Matthew Montemore, an associate professor of chemical engineering, both in Tulane's Department of Chemical & Biomolecular Engineering, according to [SciTechDaily](https://scitechdaily.com/scientists-finally-uncover-why-gold-never-tarnishes/), which cites a publication date of May 21, 2026.

The researchers used computer simulations to model how atoms and electrons behave when oxygen molecules encounter gold's surface, according to [ScienceDaily](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/07/260710003511.htm). "People have generally thought gold doesn't tarnish simply because it doesn't interact strongly with oxygen," Montemore said, according to [Phys.org](https://phys.org/news/2026-05-gold-glitter-uncover-resists-tarnish.html). "What we show is that for two of the most common gold surface types, the surface atoms actually rearrange themselves in a way that makes the gold much more resistant to oxidation."

According to [Science News](https://www.sciencenews.org/article/physics-explains-gold-shiny-oxidize), gold atoms rearrange from square lattice arrangements into hexagonal patterns: the square configuration readily splits oxygen molecules, while the hexagonal structure creates a barrier, since oxygen-splitting would first require the hexagons to distort back into squares. Montemore described the effect in stark terms: "It's something like a billion to a trillion times slower oxidation once you rearrange," he told [Science News](https://www.sciencenews.org/article/physics-explains-gold-shiny-oxidize), adding that "the tiny position shifts make a tremendous difference."

[Scientific American](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/scientists-discover-why-gold-doesnt-rust/) reports the mechanism differently framed: gold's surface atoms rearrange into a zigzag "herringbone" configuration through a process called surface reconstruction, and oxygen molecules dissociate and bind more readily before that restructuring occurs. Once the herringbone pattern forms, the surface becomes denser and closer to thermodynamic equilibrium, making it substantially harder for oxygen to penetrate. Biswas summed up the motivation for the research to Scientific American: "Everyone knows that gold is difficult to oxidize. The thing is, why? What is the proper reason for that?"

The findings point toward practical applications beyond explaining gold's shine. According to the [EurekAlert](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1129141) release from Tulane, the work could inform the design of gold-palladium catalysts used in vinyl acetate production, carbon monoxide removal from vehicle exhaust, and propylene oxide manufacturing. Montemore also suggested a route to turning gold's inertness on its head: "If you can trick gold into dissociating oxygen, it can actually become a very effective catalyst for certain reactions," he said, according to [Phys.org](https://phys.org/news/2026-05-gold-glitter-uncover-resists-tarnish.html). "Our work suggests a new strategy for potentially doing that by preventing or reversing these surface rearrangements."

## What We Don't Know

The secondary coverage reviewed does not specify which crystallographic surface orientations were modeled beyond describing them as "two of the most common gold surface types," nor does it detail the simulation methods beyond describing them broadly as calculations of atomic and electronic behavior. It is also not yet clear how quickly, if at all, the proposed strategy of "preventing or reversing" surface reconstruction could be translated into a working industrial catalyst.

## Analysis

The result reframes a question that has quietly nagged materials scientists: gold's reputation for chemical inertness has long been treated as an intrinsic property of the metal, but this study locates the real cause in a dynamic, geometry-driven response of the surface itself. That distinction matters for catalysis research, where gold is prized for selectivity in reactions like vinyl acetate synthesis, per [EurekAlert](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1129141) — if the same reconstruction that keeps gold shiny can be selectively suppressed or reversed, it opens a design lever for tuning gold-based catalysts rather than treating their reactivity as fixed.
